Bloodhound 2019

By: Diana Lucas | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Bloodhound LSR, the most powerful straight-line car on the planet is about to leave the UK. Destination, South Africa Hakskeenpan desert in the Northern Cape. This is in preparation to break the land speed record of 763.035mph or 1,227,9km/h, this was the record set in 1997 by United Kingdom team Richard Noble and the car driven by Andy Green.

Land Speed Record Holder, Andy Green (who was a serving officer in the Royal Air Force) will be the driver to break his own record and will be here to put the car through it’s final
tests, in a series of high speed shakedowns in the pan.

Between mid- October and mid-November, Andy will be building up speed in over 13 test runs culminating in mind-blowing speeds of over 500mph (800+km/h). That’s as fast as a commercial airlines cruising speed but on solid ground and would put the Bloodhound as one of the 10 fastest cars of all time.


Further information:
The speed they want to eventually break the world record with is 1000 mph and this they aim to do in 12 – 18 month’s time back at the pan.

The Bloodhound Project we filmed seven years ago. We were at the pan, filming from a plane the pan at the speed they projected the car would be going at. But the car wasn’t even built and the project exhausted funds and had huge administration problems and died. In December it was rescued from administration and has been back on track.

Bloodhound CEO Ian Warhurst: “I’ve really enjoyed watching the team rise to the challenge over these past 6 months. Something which has been talked about and planned for so long is now really happening – and the team have taken it in their stride.”

This stage of the testing is crucial, the 300- 500mph window is one of the most vulnerable stages for the car. It’s at this point that the stability of the car transitions by being governed by the interaction of the wheels on the desert surface to being actually controlled by the car’s aerodynamics…its at this point the car becomes it’s least stable.

This is the full dress rehearsal for the record –breaking campaign, the team will develop their operational procedures, perfect they work together and with the car in the desert and test all the radio communications.

The Bloodhound car is a combination of fast jet, F1 car and spaceship, at full speed it could cover 1.6km in 3.6 seconds, that’s 4.5 soccer pitches laid end to end, per second or 150m in the blink of an eye.

But other than aiming to set a new land speed record, the project is also an “international education initiative aimed at inspiring the next generation of scientists, engineers and mathematicians in the most exciting way possible”.
It’s a supersonic test bed for showcasing emergent digital technologies. The project is being followed in over 220 countries and territories.
Hakskeenpan in the Northern Cape was chosen as the best site out of many potentials in the world, now destined to become the world’s fastest track.
A team of 300 previously unemployed people funded by the Northern Cape government joined some volunteers to clear 10 million square metres of desert race track.
Andy Green when he first visited said: “I’m standing in the middle of the Hakskeenpan on a perfectly cloudless winter's day and looking 10 km in each direction I’m standing in the middle of what is rapidly becoming the world’s best race track. The team of 300 South African workers has now finished clearing the main track and is now preparing the safety areas”.

Bloodhound CEO Ian Warhurst “It’s also very important to remember that the team in South Africa have also risen to the challenge. After so much work and several false starts, the Northern Cape Provincial Government didn’t hesitate to re-engage and have worked quickly and efficiently to help us finalise agreements and then mobilise the local workforce. This in return has brought much needed employment to the area to help us clear and prepare the track.
“So that’s it – we are off to South Africa to start putting the car through its paces. This is engineering at its best and I look forward to everyone joining us online as the action unfolds this autumn.”

All the tests will be filmed, we will have B-Roll footage of the full five weeks. To get the interviews and best testing the 8-9th November will be the best time to be there.

This is a real man’s story filled with fascinating techie detail and car firsts.

The cars solid aluminium wheels are being used for the first time, they are specialty designed for the desert. Measuring 900 mm in diameter and weighing 95kg each, they are designed to spin up to 10,200 rpm (revolutions per minute) – more than four timed faster than wheels on a Formula1 car at top speed. As the car gather speed the wheels will rise up out of the mud surface in much the same way as a speedboat rides on the surface of the water, at 804 km/h and above only a few millimeters of the metal will be in contact with the desert surface, acting more like rudders than wheels on a conventional car.

There are also scientific first happening, as data on the interaction between the solid aluminium wheels, coupled with ‘base drag’ measurements will provide real world insight into the power required to set records.

Explanation: Base drag relates to the aerodynamic force produced by low pressure at the rear of the car, sucking it back. As the car approaches transonic speeds, this force far exceeds the friction of the air passing over Bloodhound’s bodywork. 

Assistant Aerospace Engineering Professor Ben Evans from Swansea University and PhD student Jack Townsend will be at Hakskeenpan to analyse the performance data from each of the runs. Comparing this real data it to the predicted computer models and see how closely they marry up. This will improve the accuracy of future modelling.

A Roll’s Royce EJ200 jet engine is powering Bloodhound, this is an engine normally found on the Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet, hugely powerful with 9 tonnes of thrust equivalent to about 54,000 thrust horsepower – this is equal to the combined output of 360 family cars.
Final jet installation check before dispatch to South Africa for high speed testing
Prior to departure there are a series of tests which we will have access to the footage, ‘dry crank’ the state of the art engine to check all the systems are correct and working perfectly. This is a crucial part of the pre-testing programme as it confirms the engine and all it’s ancillary systems, fuels and electrics are correctly installed and ready to fire up. To perform the test the team will use a small jet engine to blow high pressure air into the Aircraft Mounted Accessories Drive (AMAD) gearbox which will both spin the jet’s turbine up to the required speed and once spinning, generate3-phase AC power for the car, which then sends power to the jet engine’s fuel pumps.
Moving the 6.4 tonne Bloodhound 9,000 kms to South Africa is a major logistical challenge. Most of the heavy support system including the car’s trailer has already left the UK on a boat but the precious Bloodhound will travel via airfreight to ensure it isn’t subjected to any uncontrolled shock loads that could damage it in transit.

Bloodhound LSR Engineering Director Mark Chapman said: “Transforming Bloodhound from a runway spec car to one capable of reaching speeds in the transonic range on the desert racetrack has been no small task. The team of engineers, craftsmen, fabricators and technicians have pulled out all the stops to upgrade the car in just a few months since the rescue from administration last December.
“After many years in preparation, we can’t wait to get out to the Hakskeenpan and let Bloodhound off the leash to see just how it performs.”

Two Travel Days as per Wynand and editorial team
Flight to Upington as per Wynand and editorial team

Script:




Link: This is Hakskeen Pan in the northern Cape...about 250 kms from Upington. It's dry, dusty and remote.  But if all goes according to plan...IT will soon be the focus of the world's media 

V/O
Bloodhound LSR, a jet and rocket powered car, designed to go faster than the speed of sound is being put though it’s final paces in a series of high speed test runs on this vast pan.

Andy : We looked all over the world for the best surface we could find to run on, the very last place we came to the Northern Cape, the Verneuk Pan was good and we looked at the Hakskeen pan which was the best. This was our choice.

V/O
The man behind the wheel of Bloodhound is Andy Green a fighter pilot who set the land speed record of 1.227.9 km/h back in 1997. A record he still holds.

Andy This is the first straight line racing car of the digital age. We can have an engineering adventure here that can push back the boundaries of physics do something that no one has ever done before and share that with a global audience of 10’s of millions of people while we are doing it.

Link: Bloodhound car LSR is a combination of fast jet, F1 car and spaceship and at its projected top speed it will be almost twice as fast as a commercial airliner.

V/O
Now the plan is to break his own land speed record on this pan in about a year’s time….but this visit is all about putting Bloodhound through a series of tests to see how it runs

Derek: What is it like to drive or pilot what do you call it?
Andy: Surprisingly not as noisy as you would expect the faster you go you leave the jet noise behind you you are literally running away from it.

V/O
This brave British Project was first announced in 2008 to shatter the world land speed record. When we met up with them here on this pan five years ago, they were humbled at how the Siyanda District population had cleared the pan of over 6 000 tons of stones.

Andy: The Northern Cape and the local near communities here were challenged a decade ago to prepare the worlds best straight line racing track and that’s exactly what they have done.

V/O
But the project ran out of a money a year ago, it was Yorkshire businessman Ian Warhurst who saved Bloodhound literally a day before the car was due to be sent to the scrapyard.

Ian: So it was a crying shame that a project like that was going to go to waste and all of the hard work of the last 10 years would basically end up in a skip.
Derek: You saved the Bloodhound by one day?
Ian: Literally ya I realized if I didn’t do a deal with the administrator their and then and I went home and left some doubt about it then the next person in the door was the man with the saw

V/O
We were on the pan for their eighth test run.

Mark: When I am here I want things to go wrong.

V/O
Engineering Director Mark Chapman has been on the project from the beginning, he is responsible for the car.

Derek: What have you got to say about the testing so far?
Mark: So this is not really about speed, we have achieved 500 mph, 800km so that was really our target so that’s we are all testing systems the next thing we are gong to be testing is the airbrakes, you see them on the side of the car so you just have to do the test with that see how they work. So this whole test is not about speed about slowing down.

V/O
There is a gaping whole at the back of Bloodhound… next year a rocket will fill this gap to give extra thrust to reach the speed of 1 300 kmh.

Link: The solid aluminium wheels have been designed for the desert surface and to spin four times faster than a Formula one car at full speed, Lewis Hamilton you would get left in the dust

Andy: With the solid metal wheels we have to use at these speeds it’s like driving, after a long dry period having a massive down pour of rain it’s a really slippery road to drive on that’s what it feels like at slow speed. When the car goes faster it actually gets worse and I can feel above 300 km/h the car actually starts to move around and I have to be really delicate and precise with the steering to keep the car tracking straight down the track.
Derek: The wheels almost become rudders?
Andy Pretty much so and the faster we go the more that aerodynamic affect starts to control the car but as we are going faster the mechanical grip has already disappeared. So particularly out here in the desert in the middle of the day we get gusts of thermal winds cross winds the car will literally float from side to side and I am pulling it back all the time.

Link: You would think a project like this would be planned behind closed doors...but it's just the opposite. Bloodhound is a showcase for the latest technology and innovation

V/O
Bloodhound’s open source on line platform, gets people around the world to engage with the science and technology of the project allowing specialists and students to fuse their scientific skills.

Ian: this project isn’t just about breaking a LSR, this is about inspiring people to do engineering because when you look at the bigger picture you ask yourself why are we sending a jet rocket car down the desert what is the good of that to the world the world has got a lot of problems, environmental problems and they are going to be solved I believe by engineering and scientists coming up with new things
We are not going to stop flying around the world what we need to do is learn how to travel carbon neutral that’s the solution and we are going to get that by designing new things and getting new ways of doing things and that’s what scientists and engineers are going to do,

LINK: They are ready to roll out for the 8th run of Bloodhound in SA going for 550 miles an hour its like a well oiled military operation but its also when things can go wrong.

V/O
Air Traffic Controller, Jess Kinsman ensures the safe running of Bloodhound on the 16 km track.

Derek: So you are really the voice of Bloodhound?
Jess: I am the voice, I am the voice of control out there we have a 16 km track and as you can see you cannot see a km or two ahead of you so we work on a procedural basis here to make sure the track, stays safe so everybody that goes out on the track has to get clearance from the control room and then we monitor where every body is on the tracks based on the calls that we make.
Derek: Who gives the final countdown?
Jess: We have a number of Bloodhound team marshalls at this side of the track all of the SA guys on the West side of the track so they will all radio in and say their areas are clear. The rescue vehicles are all in place the marshalls are all in place, once everything lines up then we are good to go.

Link: There’s a strange sort of calm out here on the pan just before Bloodhound blasts off off. Final checks and adjustments Andy Green will soon be climbing into the cockpit and once they are ready for blast off we will be told to clear the area get to a safe zone.

V/O
Jess gives the go ahead and Bloodhound tears down runway, creating a sandstorm in it’s wake.

Their aim today to achieve 880 kmp/h falls just short..……with a warning of overheating in the engine, Andy played it safe.

Andy Tempting to just ignore it and get to 880, the right thing to do we got to about 800 km/h shut the car down, minor overheat to look at everything else fine.

V//O
It took another couple of days, adjustments done and Bloodhound went back on the track…. And achieved a new top speed of 1010 km per hour as she passed the 8 km mark in just 50 seconds


V/O
It’s mission accomplished for the team, until late next year when Green is confident he will make history and break his own land speed record.

V/O There is a gaping whole at the back of Bloodhound… next year a rocket will fill this gap to give extra thrust to reach the speed of 1 300 kmh. Link: The solid aluminium wheels have been designed for the desert surface and to spin four times faster than a Formula one car at full speed, Lewis Hamilton you would get left in the dust Andy: With the solid metal wheels we have to use at these speeds it’s like driving, after a long dry period having a massive down pour of rain it’s a really slippery road to drive on that’s what it feels like at slow speed. When the car goes faster it actually gets worse and I can feel above 300 km/h the car actually starts to move around and I have to be really delicate and precise with the steering to keep the car tracking straight down the track. Derek: The wheels almost become rudders? Andy Pretty much so and the faster we go the more that aerodynamic affect starts to control the car but as we are going faster the mechanical grip has already disappeared. So particularly out here in the desert in the middle of the day we get gusts of thermal winds cross winds the car will literally float from side to side and I am pulling it back all the time. Link: You would think a project like this would be planned behind closed doors...but it's just the opposite. Bloodhound is a showcase for the latest technology and innovation V/O Bloodhound’s open source on line platform, gets people around the world to engage with the science and technology of the project allowing specialists and students to fuse their scientific skills. Ian: this project isn’t just about breaking a LSR, this is about inspiring people to do engineering because when you look at the bigger picture you ask yourself why are we sending a jet rocket car down the desert what is the good of that to the world the world has got a lot of problems, environmental problems and they are going to be solved I believe by engineering and scientists coming up with new things We are not going to stop flying around the world what we need to do is learn how to travel carbon neutral that’s the solution and we are going to get that by designing new things and getting new ways of doing things and that’s what scientists and engineers are going to do, LINK: They are ready to roll out for the 8th run of Bloodhound in SA going for 550 miles an hour its like a well oiled military operation but its also when things can go wrong. V/O Air Traffic Controller, Jess Kinsman ensures the safe running of Bloodhound on the 16 km track. Derek: So you are really the voice of Bloodhound? Jess: I am the voice, I am the voice of control out there we have a 16 km track and as you can see you cannot see a km or two ahead of you so we work on a procedural basis here to make sure the track, stays safe so everybody that goes out on the track has to get clearance from the control room and then we monitor where every body is on the tracks based on the calls that we make. Derek: Who gives the final countdown? Jess: We have a number of Bloodhound team marshalls at this side of the track all of the SA guys on the West side of the track so they will all radio in and say their areas are clear. The rescue vehicles are all in place the marshalls are all in place, once everything lines up then we are good to go. Link: There’s a strange sort of calm out here on the pan just before Bloodhound blasts off off. Final checks and adjustments Andy Green will soon be climbing into the cockpit and once they are ready for blast off we will be told to clear the area get to a safe zone. V/O Jess gives the go ahead and Bloodhound tears down runway, creating a sandstorm in it’s wake. Their aim today to achieve 880 kmp/h falls just short..……with a warning of overheating in the engine, Andy played it safe. Andy Tempting to just ignore it and get to 880, the right thing to do we got to about 800 km/h shut the car down, minor overheat to look at everything else fine. V//O It took another couple of days, adjustments done and Bloodhound went back on the track…. And achieved a new top speed of 1010 km per hour as she passed the 8 km mark in just 50 seconds V/O It’s mission accomplished for the team, until late next year when Green is confident he will make history and break his own land speed record.

metadata.Summary: Bloodhound LSR, the most powerful straight-line car on the planet is about to leave the UK. Destination, South Africa Hakskeenpan desert in the Northern Cape. This is in preparation to break the land speed record of 763.035mph or 1,227,9km/h, this was the record set in 1997 by United Kingdom team Richard Noble and the car driven by Andy Green. Land Speed Record Holder, Andy Green (who was a serving officer in the Royal Air Force) will be the driver to break his own record and will be here to put the car through it’s final tests, in a series of high speed shakedowns in the pan. Between mid- October and mid-November, Andy will be building up speed in over 13 test runs culminating in mind-blowing speeds of over 500mph (800+km/h). That’s as fast as a commercial airlines cruising speed but on solid ground and would put the Bloodhound as one of the 10 fastest cars of all time.
metadata.Further information: The speed they want to eventually break the world record with is 1000 mph and this they aim to do in 12 – 18 month’s time back at the pan. The Bloodhound Project we filmed seven years ago. We were at the pan, filming from a plane the pan at the speed they projected the car would be going at. But the car wasn’t even built and the project exhausted funds and had huge administration problems and died. In December it was rescued from administration and has been back on track. Bloodhound CEO Ian Warhurst: “I’ve really enjoyed watching the team rise to the challenge over these past 6 months. Something which has been talked about and planned for so long is now really happening – and the team have taken it in their stride.” This stage of the testing is crucial, the 300- 500mph window is one of the most vulnerable stages for the car. It’s at this point that the stability of the car transitions by being governed by the interaction of the wheels on the desert surface to being actually controlled by the car’s aerodynamics…its at this point the car becomes it’s least stable. This is the full dress rehearsal for the record –breaking campaign, the team will develop their operational procedures, perfect they work together and with the car in the desert and test all the radio communications. The Bloodhound car is a combination of fast jet, F1 car and spaceship, at full speed it could cover 1.6km in 3.6 seconds, that’s 4.5 soccer pitches laid end to end, per second or 150m in the blink of an eye. But other than aiming to set a new land speed record, the project is also an “international education initiative aimed at inspiring the next generation of scientists, engineers and mathematicians in the most exciting way possible”. It’s a supersonic test bed for showcasing emergent digital technologies. The project is being followed in over 220 countries and territories. Hakskeenpan in the Northern Cape was chosen as the best site out of many potentials in the world, now destined to become the world’s fastest track. A team of 300 previously unemployed people funded by the Northern Cape government joined some volunteers to clear 10 million square metres of desert race track. Andy Green when he first visited said: “I’m standing in the middle of the Hakskeenpan on a perfectly cloudless winter's day and looking 10 km in each direction I’m standing in the middle of what is rapidly becoming the world’s best race track. The team of 300 South African workers has now finished clearing the main track and is now preparing the safety areas”. Bloodhound CEO Ian Warhurst “It’s also very important to remember that the team in South Africa have also risen to the challenge. After so much work and several false starts, the Northern Cape Provincial Government didn’t hesitate to re-engage and have worked quickly and efficiently to help us finalise agreements and then mobilise the local workforce. This in return has brought much needed employment to the area to help us clear and prepare the track. “So that’s it – we are off to South Africa to start putting the car through its paces. This is engineering at its best and I look forward to everyone joining us online as the action unfolds this autumn.” All the tests will be filmed, we will have B-Roll footage of the full five weeks. To get the interviews and best testing the 8-9th November will be the best time to be there. This is a real man’s story filled with fascinating techie detail and car firsts. The cars solid aluminium wheels are being used for the first time, they are specialty designed for the desert. Measuring 900 mm in diameter and weighing 95kg each, they are designed to spin up to 10,200 rpm (revolutions per minute) – more than four timed faster than wheels on a Formula1 car at top speed. As the car gather speed the wheels will rise up out of the mud surface in much the same way as a speedboat rides on the surface of the water, at 804 km/h and above only a few millimeters of the metal will be in contact with the desert surface, acting more like rudders than wheels on a conventional car. There are also scientific first happening, as data on the interaction between the solid aluminium wheels, coupled with ‘base drag’ measurements will provide real world insight into the power required to set records. Explanation: Base drag relates to the aerodynamic force produced by low pressure at the rear of the car, sucking it back. As the car approaches transonic speeds, this force far exceeds the friction of the air passing over Bloodhound’s bodywork. Assistant Aerospace Engineering Professor Ben Evans from Swansea University and PhD student Jack Townsend will be at Hakskeenpan to analyse the performance data from each of the runs. Comparing this real data it to the predicted computer models and see how closely they marry up. This will improve the accuracy of future modelling. A Roll’s Royce EJ200 jet engine is powering Bloodhound, this is an engine normally found on the Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet, hugely powerful with 9 tonnes of thrust equivalent to about 54,000 thrust horsepower – this is equal to the combined output of 360 family cars. Final jet installation check before dispatch to South Africa for high speed testing Prior to departure there are a series of tests which we will have access to the footage, ‘dry crank’ the state of the art engine to check all the systems are correct and working perfectly. This is a crucial part of the pre-testing programme as it confirms the engine and all it’s ancillary systems, fuels and electrics are correctly installed and ready to fire up. To perform the test the team will use a small jet engine to blow high pressure air into the Aircraft Mounted Accessories Drive (AMAD) gearbox which will both spin the jet’s turbine up to the required speed and once spinning, generate3-phase AC power for the car, which then sends power to the jet engine’s fuel pumps. Moving the 6.4 tonne Bloodhound 9,000 kms to South Africa is a major logistical challenge. Most of the heavy support system including the car’s trailer has already left the UK on a boat but the precious Bloodhound will travel via airfreight to ensure it isn’t subjected to any uncontrolled shock loads that could damage it in transit. Bloodhound LSR Engineering Director Mark Chapman said: “Transforming Bloodhound from a runway spec car to one capable of reaching speeds in the transonic range on the desert racetrack has been no small task. The team of engineers, craftsmen, fabricators and technicians have pulled out all the stops to upgrade the car in just a few months since the rescue from administration last December. “After many years in preparation, we can’t wait to get out to the Hakskeenpan and let Bloodhound off the leash to see just how it performs.”
